content: Babesiosis is a disease caused by microscopic parasites that infect red blood cells. These parasites are organisms that live inside or on another organism to survive. While there are many species of Babesia parasites that infect animals, only a few are known to infect humans. In the United States, the most common species responsible for human infection is Babesia microti. Many individuals infected with babesiosis may not experience any symptoms or feel unwell. However, some people may develop flu-like symptoms, which can include fever, chills, sweating, headaches, body aches, loss of appetite, nausea, and fatigue. Since the parasites target red blood cells, babesiosis can lead to a condition called hemolytic anemia. Hemolytic anemia occurs when red blood cells are destroyed faster than the body can replace them. This condition can become severe or even life-threatening in certain groups of people, particularly those who do not have a spleen, have weakened immune systems (due to conditions like cancer, lymphoma, or HIV), have serious underlying health issues such as liver or kidney disease, or are older than 50 years of age. If symptoms occur, they typically begin about a week after infection but may take several weeks, months, or even longer to develop. In the United States, most cases of babesiosis are transmitted through the bite of blacklegged ticks, also known as deer ticks (Ixodes scapularis). These ticks are commonly found in wooded, brushy, or grassy areas. The majority of cases occur in the Northeast and upper Midwest regions of the country. Less commonly, babesiosis can be transmitted through blood transfusions from an infected donor or from an infected mother to her baby during pregnancy or delivery. It is important to note that Babesia parasites are not spread from person to person through casual contact, such as coughing or sneezing. To prevent babesiosis, it is essential to minimize exposure to tick-infested areas. If you are in such areas, use tick repellents, wear protective clothing such as long-sleeved shirts, pants, and socks, and thoroughly check yourself and your pets for ticks before entering your home. Babesiosis can be diagnosed by a healthcare provider through laboratory testing. A small sample of blood can be examined under a microscope to detect the presence of Babesia parasites within red blood cells. Alternatively, blood samples can be sent to specialized laboratories, such as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) or a state health department, for confirmation. Effective treatment is available for babesiosis. In cases where individuals do not exhibit symptoms or signs of the disease, treatment may not be necessary. However, it is important to consult with a healthcare provider to determine the appropriate course of action based on individual circumstances.
